parsed_refs.title: Coronary slow flow: is it a disease or normal variant?

raw_text:
The coronary slow flow phenomenon (CSFP) is an angiographic entity in which contrast opacification of the distal coronary bed is delayed despite absent obstructive epicardial coronary artery disease. Since its first description in 1972 [1], CSFP has evolved from an angiographic curiosity to a clinically relevant syndrome linked to recurrent angina, objective ischemia, acute coronary syndrome (ACS)-like presentations, arrhythmias, and impaired quality of life [3-5]. Contemporary diagnosis relies on objective coronary flow assessment, particularly the corrected thrombolysis in myocardial infarction frame count (CTFC), introduced by Gibson et al. [2]. Many studies define CSFP as CTFC >27 frames at 30 frames/s in at least one major epicardial artery, after excluding secondary causes such as epicardial stenosis, spasm, ectasia, embolism, myocardial bridging, left ventricular dysfunction, valvular disease, or recent percutaneous coronary intervention [4,6].

Reported prevalence varies because of differences in referral populations and definitions. In angiographic series it is usually found in approximately 1–7% of diagnostic angiograms [6,14,15]. Hawkins et al. reported CSFP in 5.5% of consecutive patients undergoing angiography, with male sex and obesity as independent correlates [6]. Other cohorts emphasize hypertension, dyslipidemia, low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, smoking, metabolic risk, and higher hemoglobin as associated features [14,15]. Clinically, CSFP is over-represented among relatively younger men and smokers, but it is not confined to this phenotype. Presentations range from stable or atypical angina to unstable angina, non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction, ST-elevation-like episodes, syncope, and ventricular arrhythmia [7,17-20]. Thus, the disorder overlaps with, but is not identical to, microvascular angina and ischemia with non-obstructive coronary arteries.

Pathophysiology is multifactorial. Histopathological data from endomyocardial biopsy demonstrated luminal narrowing, vessel-wall thickening, endothelial swelling, and degenerative microvascular changes in patients with otherwise normal epicardial arteries [3]. Invasive physiological studies further suggest increased resting microvascular tone, reduced coronary sinus oxygen saturation, and abnormal vasodilator responses [5]. However, CSFP is not always synonymous with reduced coronary flow reserve: Fineschi et al. found preserved hyperemic reserve despite increased resting microvascular resistance, implying that elevated basal tone may be central in some patients [10]. Endothelial dysfunction is also prominent; brachial flow-mediated dilation is reduced in CSFP [8], and circulating adhesion molecules are increased, supporting endothelial activation and inflammation [11]. Biomarker studies implicate homocysteine, asymmetric dimethylarginine, resistin, and platelet activation, although findings are heterogeneous and not yet clinically decisive [12,13,24,26,27].

A second mechanism is diffuse, angiographically occult atherosclerosis. Intravascular ultrasound studies demonstrated diffuse intimal thickening and calcification despite apparently normal angiograms [9]. More recent work combining coronary flow reserve and hidden atherosclerosis assessment supports the concept that some “slow flow” reflects diffuse non-obstructive epicardial disease rather than isolated microvascular dysfunction [28]. Coronary anatomy may also contribute: tortuosity, branching, and vessel geometry correlate with CTFC and may promote disturbed laminar flow, endothelial injury, and delayed contrast transit [29]. These observations explain why CSFP should be considered a phenotype rather than a single disease mechanism.

Evaluation begins during angiography. Quantitative CTFC is preferable to visual TIMI flow grading because it improves reproducibility [2]. The left anterior descending count should be corrected for vessel length. Clinicians should document the vessels involved, exclude secondary causes, and integrate symptoms, electrocardiographic changes, troponin results, and left ventricular function. Non-invasive ischemia testing may be positive, but perfusion results are variable [7,20]. Because CSFP may coexist with risk factors and subclinical atherosclerosis, cardiovascular risk assessment is warranted even when angiography is “normal.”

Management remains empiric. Lifestyle and risk-factor control—smoking cessation, weight optimization, blood pressure and lipid management, glycemic control, and exercise—are reasonable because of the frequent association with metabolic and atherosclerotic risk [6,14,15]. Antianginal therapy targets microvascular tone. Dipyridamole improved angiographic flow in early studies [22]. Calcium-channel blockade is supported by small trials: mibefradil improved TIMI flow and angina frequency before withdrawal of the drug from markets [21], and sustained-release diltiazem improved symptoms and angiographic parameters at 6 months [23]. Case series suggest that intracoronary or oral calcium-channel blockers may be useful in acute or recurrent chest pain syndromes, although high-quality evidence is limited [17,23]. Other approaches, including hyperbaric oxygen, statins, beta-blockers with nitric-oxide-mediated effects, nicorandil, ranolazine, and antiplatelet strategies, remain investigational or based on small studies [24,25].

Prognosis is usually favorable regarding mortality, but CSFP is not benign. Recurrent chest pain, repeat admissions, repeated angiography, ACS-like presentations, ventricular arrhythmias, and rare sudden death have been reported [16,18,19]. The key clinical message is that CSFP should prompt neither dismissal nor overdiagnosis: it is an angiographic marker of abnormal coronary vascular function, often reflecting a mixture of microvascular constriction, endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, altered rheology, and occult atherosclerosis. Future studies should standardize diagnostic thresholds, phenotype patients by invasive and non-invasive physiology, and test mechanism-based therapy in adequately powered randomized trials [4,16,30].
